PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349


APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES§

BEFORE THE

STATE OFF OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS


INTERVENOR SUSAN BURROW’S
REPLY BRIEF 

This filing is drafted from the admitted record references, exhibit references, hearing transcript references, and initial post-hearing briefs provided in the combined intervenor brief compilations and Applicants' Initial Post-Hearing Brief. It is written as a consolidated merits brief preserving denial, deferral, route exclusion, procedural, and alternative-relief arguments raised by affected landowners and aligned intervenors.

TABLE OF CONTENTS
I. INTRODUCTION
II. ARGUMENTS 
     A.  Evidence of Need is Questionable and Not Proven
     B.  Public Meeting Notice Failures and Non-Compliance of TAC 22.52 Intent
     C.  The 1,400 Landowners and Late-Notice Route Exclusion Recommendation
     D.  Import Path 2 Timing, 2038 
     E.  Need, HB 5066, and ERCOT Forecast Reliability
     F.   Alternatives Analysis and Generation Alternatives
     G.  180-Day Schedule, Due Process, and Intervenor Dismissals
     H.  Habitable Structure Errors, Travel Trailers, And Route Scoring Impacts
     I.  Prudent Avoidance, Schools, Churches, and Human 
     J.  Community Values, Historic Resources, Ranching, Water, and Tribal Interests
     K.  QA/QC, Field Verification, Pipeline, and Environmental 
     L.  Route Development Deficiencies, and Link-Specific Evidence 
     M.  Response to Applicant's Initial Brief
III.   SUMMARY OF ARGUMENTS
XX. Prayer for Relief

I. Introduction
This highly contested case concerns the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to amend their certificates of convenience and necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV transmission line project. If approved, the Applicants gain the authority to construct an unprecedented 765-kV line across fifteen Texas counties, impose permanent 200 ft. easements, clear wide rights-of-way, scar private rural land forever, and transfer a significant amount of the costs to Texas ratepayers.
The Applicants filed the Application on March 26, 2026. In their Initial Post-Hearing Brief, Applicants state that the Application includes cost estimates for 122 geographically diverse routes comprised of 171 alternative route links, documentation supporting need. Applicants also state that the 122 routes span approximately 200 miles east-to-west and 35 miles north-to-south and that additional routes can be formed from noticed links. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 11-13).
Throughout this process, there has been an unprecedented amount of public concern. Applicants' own brief confirms that more than 1,600 individuals and entities requested intervention and that more than 700 statements of position and witness direct testimonies were filed on behalf of intervenors. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 7-8).  It's clear that this is a project with consequences so broad that ordinary landowners, churches, schools, ranching families, counties, tribes, and small businesses sought to be heard despite a compressed schedule and an exceptionally technical process.  
Per the instructions for this process, I have based my arguments on points, and discussions that were included in the Docket, and in the Hearing.  

II. ARGUMENTS
A.  EVIDENCE OF NEED IS QUESTIONABLE AND NOT PROVEN
Throughout this process, there has been a tremendous of concern about the actual need of all three import paths, and how soon they were actually needed.  Applicants ask the ALJs and the Commission to treat the Commission's prior approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and ERCOT's import-path modeling as sufficient proof of need in this docket. Applicants further argue that the Application and notice were found sufficient, that the public participation process was adequate, and that any of the 122 filed routes can be approved. 
The case for the Applicants' need relies heavily on the proposition that ERCOT recommended the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, and that the Commission approved the plan.  Applicants' Initial Brief states that the Project was recommended by ERCOT in the PBRP, that the Commission approved the PBRP in Project No. 55718, and that a later Commission order approved the 765-kV import paths. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 3-5).
That background does not satisfy the burden of CCN. The issue is not whether a planning process occurred. The issue is whether the Applicants proved in this docket that this particular 765-kV project is necessary now, at this scale, on this record, through these counties, with these routes, and with the blatant public participation defects
In my, and in other Intervenors' opinions, Applicants failed to carry their burden under PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101. The record does not contain a reliable, current, quantified showing of the amount of power needing to be transported.  The claimed need, based on ERCOT modeling and PBRP assumptions has been challenged by Intervenors as outdated, speculative, and not validated against actual load materialization.
The need is undermined by evidence a substantial portion of the projected non-oil-and-gas load was cryptocurrency mining load; and data centers, and that ERCOT has since adopted more conservative forecasting methods; and that Senate Bill 6 reflects legislative concern over speculative large-load interconnection requests. (Judy Graci Initial Brief, Item No. 6324).  At the risk of being objected to, there is President Trump's recent directive that data centers bring, or generate, their own power without burdening ratepayers.  I would think this has bearing on future loads needing to be transported across the state.   
Applicants also failed to prove that new 765-kV import transmission is the only, best, or least harmful solution. Multiple intervenors raised alternatives: local generation, gas-fired generation in the Permian Basin, behind-the-meter generation, off-grid generation, hybrid solutions, and use of existing corridors. (A2 Segment Affected Landowners Coalition, Item No. 6272; American Stewards of Liberty, Item No. 6225; Graci, Item No. 6324; Noland, Item No. 6323).
Intervenors presented substantial evidence that the claimed need is unproven, stale, and not sufficiently quantified. Judy Graci's brief states that the PBRP proposes three import transmission paths totaling 1,255 miles of 765-kV line at an estimated cost of approximately $13 billion and that the claimed need rests substantially on nearly 6,900 MW of cryptocurrency mining load confirmed primarily through TSP letters rather than binding contracts. (Graci Initial Brief, Item No. 6324).
Ms. Graci further explains that ERCOT's March 1, 2024 monthly update reported that of 11,995 MW of additional non-oil-and-gas load, 38% was confirmed by binding contract, 54% only by TSP officer letter, and 8% remained unconfirmed. By the June 28, 2024 workshop, the additional non-oil-and-gas load was 11,695 MW, with 39% confirmed by contract, 54% by TSP officer letter, and 8% unconfirmed. (Graci, Item No. 6324).
Those figures matter because the Commission is being asked to approve permanent, multi-billion-dollar infrastructure based on projected load that has not been shown to have materialized and that was never tested in this docket against later-realization methods. A load forecast built substantially on officer letters rather than binding commitments cannot carry the same evidentiary weight as actual signed load commitments, actual energization, or actual peak demand.
Intervenor evidence shows that the PBRP planning assumptions remain disputed and were not adequately tested through a full alternatives analysis. The Commission should not use a prior planning order to bypass PURA § 37.056's requirement that the project be necessary and that community, environmental, routing, cost, and public-interest factors be weighed on the present record.

B.  PUBLIC MEETING NOTICE FAILURE AND NON-COMPLIANCE OF TAC 22.52 INTENT 
The public meeting notice issue is one of the strongest grounds for denial of this Application. The Applicants argue that they provided public meeting notice and that notice was found sufficient. That argument misses the point. The question is not simply whether Applicants held public meetings before filing. The question is whether all affected landowners whose property became part of the filed route network had a meaningful opportunity to participate in public meetings before route development was finalized.
Applicants admit that after public participation meetings, Kimley-Horn and Halff added, modified, and removed preliminary route links and expanded the study area in response to newly identified constraints, further analysis, and community values. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 11-12). If route links were added, modified, or removed after public meetings, then landowners affected by those later links did not receive the same public meeting opportunity as earlier landowners.
Approximately 1,400 other families were impacted by lines added after the June 2025 public meetings, that they were not properly notified under TAC 22.52.  Personally, my husband and I received notice on April 5, 2026.  We had no knowledge of this project until that day when we received the notice. The Application included over 400 miles of newly added routes that contained links G71, G72, and G73 that directly affect our property. (My Own Initial Brief, Item Nos. 6301).
Erik Gulbranson states that he is one of approximately 1,400 landowners notified after March 26, 2026 and that no notice of a public meeting, inability to secure legal representation, and shortened timelines hindered meaningful participation and due process.(Gulbranson, Item No. 6303).
Walter and Deborah McCullough state that 2,809 public meeting notices were sent and 4,215 application notices were later sent, meaning approximately 1,400 properties were unaware until after application submittal. They identify the lost opportunities: no opportunity to learn about the project, attend a public meeting, weigh in on community values, submit comments, describe property features, obtain experienced legal services, coordinate with neighbors, protect families, or defend legacies. (McCullough, Item No. 6287).
The record also reflects that approximately 1,400 affected landowners were not afforded the same public meeting opportunity as landowners identified before the June 2025 public meetings. Approximately 1,400 properties learned of the project only after the Application was filed, and well after NEW route links were added or changed. (See, e.g., Erik Gulbranson Initial Brief, Item No. 6303; Susan Burrow Initial Brief, Item Nos. 6301 and 6220; Walter and Deborah McCullough Initial Closing Argument, Item No. 6287; John Burrow Initial Brief, Item No. 6297).
The evidence also shows that route development continued after the public meetings. Applicants acknowledge that, following the public participation meetings, Kimley-Horn and Halff added, modified, and removed preliminary route links and expanded the study area in response to newly identified constraints, further analysis, and community values. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 11-12).  These modifications impacted approximately 1400 new landowners.  In this case, the Applicants failed to provide a public meeting for the 1400 landowners on the lines that were added well after the public meetings were held in June 2025.  This is a blatant non-compliance of TAC 22.52, which states that where 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application, the utility must hold a public meeting prior to filing the application.  The Applicants, after they added new routes, chose not to hold another public meeting, leaving 1400 landowners without the opportunity that TAC 22.52 is designed to provide.  Newly affected landowners, most with no legal experience, had roughly three weeks to learn what the massive project entails, and learn how to intervene, and write and submit a testimony.  In the few weeks following that, they had to learn PUC procedures, find counsel, prepare testimony, review thousands of pages, understand route tables, and participate in a technical hearing within weeks. By that time, many folks impacted could not obtain qualified legal counsel because attorneys had already by retained by other parties.  (Tracy Snell Mack, Item No. 6309; Erik Gulbranson, Item No. 6303; John Burrow, Item No. 6297; George Noelke, Item No. 6199, are just a few).

C.  THE 1,400 LANDOWNERS AND LATE-NOTICE ROUTE EXCLUSION RECOMMENDATION
The Commission should adopt a general recommendation that no route be selected if it contains property of one of the approximately 1,400 landowners who did not receive proper notice of the June 2025 public meetings or who received the Application so late that meaningful participation was materially impaired.
This relief is justified as both a procedural remedy and a route-selection principle. It will require the Commission to avoid rewarding a defective public participation process.  
Applicants argue that all 171 links were noticed using county tax roll data when the Application was filed. Application notice is not a substitute for public meeting notice. Public meeting notice occurs before the application is filed and before route-development decisions are made. Application notice merely tells landowners that the Applicants have already selected a filed route network and started a 180-day contested case.
This is prejudiced for later-added landowners, They did not receive questionnaires during public meetings; did not see the preliminary route network at the same time; did not have the same chance to identify schools, churches, stock tanks, cemeteries, habitat, pipelines, ranch operations, future developments, and community values; and did not have the same time to obtain counsel and organize route-specific coalitions.
Accordingly, the Commission should either: (1) deny the Application; or (2) exclude any route that contains a property owned by a landowner who was not afforded the same public meeting opportunity as similarly situated landowners earlier in the process.

D.  IMPORT PATH 2 TIMING AND 2038 
Intervenors preserved the argument that Import Path 2 is not needed by 2030 and that the record points to later timing, including 2038 planning assumptions. The Applicants' route-specific CCN should not be approved based on a need that has not matured. A CCN confers eminent-domain consequences now, not in 2038. If the asserted need arises later, the proper remedy is an updated record later, not immediate condemnation now.
Graci's brief explains that ERCOT's PBRP forecast was developed in early 2024 and finalized by the June 28, 2024- ERCOT workshop, has not been validated against ERCOT's subsequently adopted adjusted forecast methodology, has never been tested against actual load materialization data, and predates Senate Bill 6. (Graci, Item No. 6324). That is powerful record evidence that the need case is stale and requires update before any CCN is approved.
The record also shows that the case for need is temporally uncertain. Intervenors challenged whether Import Path 2 is needed by 2030 and argued that the relevant need may not materialize until 2038. If the need arises at all, more than a decade from now, then the Commission should not authorize immediate condemnation of private land without updated forecasts, actual load materialization data, and full review of alternatives.
Applicants' own background section distinguishes between local upgrades and import path projects. Local upgrades are described as needed to interconnect and serve projected load once power is imported into the region, while import path projects are described as needed to transfer power from other regions into the Permian Basin. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 4-5). That distinction makes quantified proof essential. Without a quantified import requirement, the Commission cannot determine whether this import path is necessary, oversized, premature, or inferior to alternatives.
A route that imposes severe landowner, school, church, cemetery, ranch, water, habitat, pipeline, or community impacts should not be used if the project benefit is uncertain, deferred, or unquantified. 

E.  HB 5066 DOES NOT MANDATE THESE SPECIFIC 765-kV LINES
HB 5066 required ERCOT and the Commission to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin region. It did not mandate a specific 765-kV transmission line, a specific route, a specific set of counties, or immediate condemnation of private property without satisfying PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC §§ 22.52 and 25.101.
Applicants' own brief states that HB 5066 directed development of a reliability plan to extend service to areas where mineral resources have been found, increase available transmission capacity to meet forecasted load, and provide infrastructure to reduce interconnection times. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 4-5). Those objectives can include transmission, but they do not exclude generation, distributed resources, load management, local upgrades, staged solutions, or updated forecasting.
The Commission must therefore reject any argument that HB 5066 removes the need to evaluate alternatives or excuses deficiencies in notice, route development, tax records, habitable-structure counts, prudent avoidance, or community values.
The ERCOT forecast is challenged on multiple grounds. First, a substantial portion of forecasted non-oil-and-gas load was supported by TSP officer letters rather than binding contracts. Second, cryptocurrency mining constituted approximately 58-59% of the additional non-oil-and-gas load during the PBRP study period. Third, ERCOT has since adopted a more conservative forecast methodology. Fourth, the forecast was not reconciled with the Bureau of Economic Geology oil-and-gas forecast commissioned by ERCOT. (Graci, Item No. 6324).
Graci states that applying ERCOT's own realization-rate methodology would reduce projected 2030 total load from 23,659 MW to approximately 18,440 MW, a reduction of more than 20%. Graci, Item No. 6324. At that reduced load level, Applicants have not demonstrated that three import paths remain necessary or that the specific Bell County East to Big Hill project is necessary now.

F.  ALTERNATIVES ANALYSIS AND GENERATION ALTERNATIVES
Applicants have not shown that new 765-kV import transmission is the only, best, or least harmful way to meet any legitimate reliability need. 
Judi Graci argues that no alternatives analysis was required or performed because the project was classified as a reliability project and therefore exempt from the economic cost-benefit analysis that would otherwise require consideration of whether local generation could meet the same need at lower cost. (Graci, Item No. 6324). 
Ms. Graci further identifies 37 planned or announced natural gas generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and Panhandle/Northwest regions, totaling approximately 39.467 GW of new generation capacity: 24 projects totaling approximately 25.162 GW in Permian counties, 9 totaling approximately 9.808 GW in the Panhandle/Northwest, and 4 totaling approximately 4.497 GW elsewhere in West Texas. (Graci Direct Testimony Ex. A; Graci, Item No. 6324).
Mr. Noland similarly argues that Texas needs generation before transmission and that thermal generation and batteries should be planned to support grid stability, winter storms, hot summers, and large loads before committing nearly $100 billion in lifetime transmission costs. (Noland, Item No. 6323).
The Commission should not approve this Application until Applicants demonstrate, on a current record, that local generation, gas generation, off-grid generation, behind-the-meter generation, staged upgrades, and other less destructive alternatives cannot meet the actual need more reasonably, reliably, and cost-effectively.

G.  180-DAY SCHEDULE, DUE PROCESS, AND INTERVENOR DISMISSALS
The compressed 180-day schedule created fundamental fairness problems, especially for late-notified, pro se, rural landowners. Applicants and experienced parties had legal counsel, consultants, engineers, environmental professionals to act as witness, and prior experience with this process. Ordinary landowners had to learn the process while defending their homes, and maintaining their businesses, ranches, schools, churches, cemeteries, and family land.
Applicants' brief confirms the procedural compression acknowledging the filing of the Application on March 26, and Intervenor forms being due on April 27, with the hearing on June 8, 2026. (Applicants' Initial Brief, Item No. 6311, pp. 6-8).  In Item 4726, the Applicants move to stike over 800 Intervenor's testimonies, suggesting their concerns over EMF exposure, harm to wildlife management operations, property devaluation, etc. were hearsay.  Sadly, more than 800 intervenors were dismissed on June 1, 2026, for failure to file testimony or a statement of position.  This Commission should not mistake this as acceptance by the landowners of the proposed route links.   Rather, they should consider that the reason for lack of testimony or statement of position is more likely due to the ordinary landowner's inability to keep up with the intimidating and overwhelming requirements of this process.  All the while, doing their best to maintain responsibilities with work, home, and family responsibilities.  
George Noelke argues that the 839 en masse intervenor dismissals negatively impacted his rights to fully litigate all issues and that the quantity of stricken intervenors reflects a need for front-end process improvements. (Noelke, Item No. 6199). The scale of dismissal is evidence that this process did not function adequately for ordinary landowners in a case of this magnitude.
Tracy Snell Mack states that landowners on Link U1 did not receive formal notice until almost mid-April 2026, with an initial April 27 deadline, leaving less than two weeks to understand the process, file intervention, find counsel, coordinate with neighbors, and prepare. (Snell Mack, Item No. 6309).
Erik Gulbranson and John Burrow  explain that late notice and lack of public meeting notice made it difficult or impossible to obtain specialized counsel because attorneys had already been retained by other parties. (Gulbranson, Item No. 6303; John Burrow, Item No. 6297).
The ALJs and Commission should not treat participation failures as landowner neglect. In a case that initially had over 1,600 attempted intervenors, hundreds of statements and testimonies, technical filings, multiple platforms, exhibit uploads, cross-rebuttal, and hearing logistics, the record demonstrates that the compressed schedule substantially impaired meaningful participation by late-notified landowners.

H.  HABITABLE STRUCTURE ERRORS, TRAVEL TRAILERS, AND ROUTE SCORING IMPACTS
Habitable-structure counts are among the most important route-selection data points. Applicants and Staff repeatedly rely upon habitable-structure counts to evaluate prudent avoidance, route comparisons, and best-meets recommendations. If those counts are incomplete, inconsistent, or inflated by inappropriate inclusions, route scoring is unreliable.
Intervenors presented arguments that Applicants failed to properly identify habitable structures and failed to account for travel trailers and other temporary, non-permanent objects treated as habitable structures. Kevin Kennedy's Initial Post-Hearing Brief demonstrates how the Applicants included travel trailers in their counts of Habitable Structures. (Kennedy, Kevin, Item No. 6317).  A travel trailer is not equivalent to a house, mobile home, school, church, or permanent habitable structure. Counting temporary travel trailers can distort route comparisons, making one route appear more burdensome and another appear less burdensome based on movable objects rather than actual long-term human exposure.
The purpose of identifying habitable structures is not to protect structures as objects. It is to protect people from avoidable exposure and land-use impacts. This point was made repeatedly in the record. Noland states that Mr. Poole explained the purpose of avoiding habitable structures was to avoid exposing humans to the power line and associated electromagnetic radiation. (Noland, Item No. 6323).
G6 Landowners Legal Fund, Aaron Howton, Jason Howton, Newman Group, Brady Creek, Colorado River Alliance, and other briefs contain substantial route-specific habitable-structure arguments. Collectively, they demonstrate that habitable-structure analysis drove route advocacy and opposition across the docket. Any error in structure identification, classification, or travel-trailer treatment therefore affects the integrity of the entire route-selection process. No route should be selected based on an incorrect structure inventory.

I.  PRUDENTS AVOIDANCE, SCHOOLS, CHURCHES, AND HUMAN EXPOSURE
Prudent avoidance requires limiting exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort. The record shows that Applicants treated prudent avoidance too mechanically, focusing on route tables and structure counts rather than the people, schools, churches, cemeteries, and community locations that would experience exposure and disruption.
Applicants overlooked Florence Elementary School and a future highway interchange on Link F34, and they made no effort to offset the line to avoid them because they were not aware of them.  PUCT Staff witness Poole explained that, from reviewing the Application, it was apparent Applicants were not aware of the elementary school or highway interchange on Link F34 and that reasonable effort should have been expended to offset the line to avoid them. Noland, Item No. 6323 (citing Interchange 6137, Hearing Transcript June 10, 2026, pp. 95-102, Poole cross by Kevin Kennedy).
Erik Gulbranson, John Burrow, Susan Burrow, G73 Landowners, and Lazy B Land Company preserve concerns regarding G71, G72, and G73, including a school/homeschool setting and multiple nearby homes. These arguments demonstrate that prudent avoidance must consider people and regular human occupancy, not merely whether an object fits a narrow structural label.
Churches and cemeteries also require careful consideration. The Rundberg Estate brief identifies Holy Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery and the Islamic Center of Jarrell near Link F41. Rundberg Estate, Item No. 6234. Other briefs raise churches, cemeteries, and historic community resources as community values and prudent avoidance concerns. A route that places 765-kV infrastructure near schools, churches, cemeteries, and gathering places without reasonable avoidance should not be selected.

J.  COMMUNITY VALUES, HISTORIC RESOURCES, RANCHING, WATER, AND TRIBAL INTERESTS
Community values are not secondary. PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101 require their consideration. Applicants' own Environmental Assessment recognizes that public meeting respondents expressed concern about routing close to habitable structures and fragmentation of private property, and comments requested minimizing removal of oak trees and protecting Texas historical sites and landmarks dating back to the 1800s. (Meyer E11, Item No. 6308 (citing Joint Applicants' Ex. 1, pp. 203-206).
Meyer E11 Intervenors argue that community values strongly oppose routes through Belton and north Salado links E6, E7, E8, E11, and E12. They identify centuries-old oak trees on Link E11 and the historic Summers Mill structure, built in 1866, used as a post office, and registered as a Texas Historical Site since 1965. (Meyer E11, Item No. 6308).
Meyer E11 also states that not one of the Routes of Interest generated by intervenors included E6, E7, E8, E11, or E12. Joint Applicants' Exs. 22 and 23; (Meyer E11, Item No. 6308). That is direct evidence of community values and route opposition.
Comanche Nation's briefs, Item Nos. 6302 and 6286, describe tribal cultural-resource concerns. Cultural resources, archeological sites, traditional lands, and historic landscapes are not adequately protected by high-level route-table statistics alone. The Commission should require meaningful cultural-resource consideration before approving any route that risks tribal or historic resources.

K.  QA/QC, FIELD VERIFICATION, PIPELINE, AND ENVIRONMENTAL DEFICIENCIES
The record demonstrates that Applicants' quality assurance and quality control were inadequate for a project of this size. The errors and omissions are not isolated. They appear across notice, route development, structure identification, schools, churches, cemeteries, water resources, pipelines, hazards, and environmental features. The strongest examples include Florence Elementary School and the future highway interchange on Link F34, Applicants overlooked and did not avoid because they were not aware of them.  The same pattern appears in briefs identifying churches, cemeteries, stock tanks, cultural resources, solar generation, pipelines, helipads, aerospace testing facilities, etc.
Pipeline safety and AC interference were presented by George Noelke and others. Mr. Noelke states that Applicants anticipate they will not be paying pipeline operators or owners for costs of necessary safety improvements, and that all routes in the Application parallel or intersect the Matterhorn Express Pipeline, as well as the Eiger Express pipeline. (Noelke, Item No. 6199). He further argues that AC mitigation costs were not quantified. The costs of AC mitigation costs required by this project should be the Applicants burden, not the landowner, or the pipeline company owning the existing lines.
Floodplain and environmental deficiencies recur in route-specific briefs involving rivers, creeks, riparian corridors, threatened species, and habitat. Rundberg identifies Texas Horned Lizard habitat and native harvester ant colonies. (Rundberg, Item No. 6234). Colorado River Alliance, Lampasas J11 Landowners, Save the Lampasas-related briefs, Brady Creek, Cherokee Creek, N12/P1, and other groups raise river, watershed, woodland, erosion, and environmental-integrity concerns. These concerns require more than desktop route review.

L.  ROUTE DEVELOPMENT DEFICIENCIES AND LINK-SPECIFIC EVIDENCE
The record contains many link-specific objections. This brief does not ask the Commission to adopt every intervenor's preferred route. Rather, it shows that the route-development process was unreliable and that numerous links should be excluded or avoided if the Application is not denied.
G71, G72, and G73. Erik Gulbranson, John Burrow, Susan Burrow, G73 Landowners, and Lazy B Land Company identify late notice, lack of public meeting opportunity, school/homeschool proximity, multiple homes, prudent avoidance failures, community values, and route-concentration/geographic-diversity problems affecting G71, G72, and G73. Item Nos. 6303, 6297, 6301, 6220, 6230, 6229.
E6, E7, E8, E11, and E12. Meyer E11, E6 Link Intervenors, CBF Ranch, and related parties oppose northern/eastern links through Belton and north Salado because of high habitable-structure counts, historic Summers Mill, centuries-old oak trees, community values, and cultural/historical impacts. (Item Nos. 6308, 6221, 6245).
Every landowner opposes the line on their land. The point is that many of the objections made on routes are based on record-supported deficiencies: schools missed, churches and cemeteries underweighted, stock tanks crossed, existing solar generation removed without quantification, pipeline AC mitigation costs omitted, hazard zones not captured, water resources under-analyzed, and public meeting participation denied.

M.  RESPONSE TO APPLICANTS' INITIAL BRIEF
Applicants' Initial Brief contains several propositions that should be rejected or limited.
Applicants argue that the Application is adequate because it includes 122 routes and 171 links. Quantity does not equal adequacy. A large set of routes can still be defective if built on incomplete notice, outdated forecasts, inaccurate structure counts, missed schools, incomplete environmental data, and inadequate QA/QC.
The Applicants argue that notice was sufficient. Yet approximately 1400 later-added landowners were not afforded the opportunity to participate in meaningful public meetings, and participation in route development. This is a blatant non-compliance of the intent of TAC 22.52(a)(4)(A).
The Applicants argue that ERCOT and the Commission already recognized need. Yet, intervenors introduced unrebutted or un-challenge concerns regarding unconfirmed load, cryptocurrency load, outdated forecast methods, 2038 timing, and alternatives.
The Applicants argue that all routes comply with PURA and TAC. Compliance requires reliable data. Where habitable structure counts, tax rolls, field verification, public participation, and route scoring are contested, the Commission should not presume compliance merely because route tables were filed.
The Applicants argue that Staff did not oppose any route and Staff recommended Route 487. Staff's recommendation is important, but the Commission must consider the whole record. Staff witnesses also acknowledged intervenor briefs, would have altered their views if certain facts such as cultural resources or school locations had been known. (Rose, Noland, Meyer E11, and other briefs).  The Applicants argue that a route can be formed from noticed links. This ignores the public meeting issue. Application notice on a link is not the same as public meeting notice and route-development participation before filing.

III. SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
In my, and in other Intervenors' opinions, Applicants failed to carry their burden of proof of need and necessity under PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101. The record does not contain a reliable, current, quantified showing of the amount of power needing to be transported.  The claimed need, based on ERCOT modeling and PBRP assumptions has been challenged by Intervenors as outdated, speculative, and not validated against actual load materialization.
The issue is not whether a planning process occurred. The issue is whether the Applicants proved in this docket that this particular 765-kV project is necessary now, at this scale, on this record, through these counties, with these routes, and with the blatant public participation defects
The public meeting process failed to satisfy the purpose and intent of 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)(A). It is not enough that public meetings occurred in June 2025 if approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners were not invited, did not receive priority-mail notice, and did not have the same opportunity to provide route-development input. The Applicants admit that route links were added, modified, and removed after public meetings.  This fact confirms that the routes outlined in the Application that was filed include new routes that impact residents that did not benefit from the public participation process available to those earlier-affected landowners.
The compressed 180-day schedule magnified the flaw in this process. Newly affected landowners had to intervene, learn PUC procedure, find counsel, prepare testimony, review thousands of pages, understand route tables, and participate in a technical hearing within weeks. Several briefs show that qualified counsel was unavailable because attorneys had already been retained by other parties. (Tracy Snell Mack, Item No. 6309; Erik Gulbranson, Item No. 6303; John Burrow, Item No. 6297; George Noelke, Item No. 6199).
The record also demonstrates deficiencies in county tax roll use, landowner identification, habitable-structure identification, travel-trailer treatment as habitable structure, GIS and parcel data, field verification, environmental review, floodplain and water-resource review, pipeline interference with no litigation costs added, hazard analysis, and route scoring. These errors are not isolated. They are systemic indicators that the route analysis was not reliable enough to support a project of this magnitude.
The Commission should deny the Application. In the alternative, the Commission should defer the project's approval; require updated ERCOT load forecasts; require new public meetings; require corrected tax roll, structure, route, environmental, and QA/QC analyses; and exclude from consideration any route containing property of one of the approximately 1,400 landowners who did not receive proper public meeting notice or who received late application notice that materially impaired meaningful participation.
The lack of meaningful participation by all affected landowners resulting from Applicant's failure to include the 1400 landowners on the new routes, as well as failure to utilize current tax roll data, resulted in a distorted and tainted route analysis and development.  This alone should disqualify the route proposal entirely.  
The Commission should adopt a general recommendation that no route be selected if it contains property of one of the approximately 1,400 landowners who did not receive proper notice of the June 2025 public meetings or who received the Application so late that meaningful participation was materially impaired.
This relief is justified as both a procedural remedy and a route-selection principle. It will require the Commission to avoid rewarding a defective public participation process.  

III. APPLICABLE PURA AND TAC STANDARDS
PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to determine whether a proposed transmission project is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. The statute requires consideration of adequacy of existing service, need for additional service, effect of granting the certificate on the recipient and any electric utility serving the proximate area, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, probable improvement of service or lowering of cost, and other factors including whether the proposed line will serve an underserved area.
16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) implements these routing factors and requires consideration of community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, engineering constraints, costs, and whether the route parallels existing compatible rights-of-way or property lines. The rule also incorporates prudent avoidance, which 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(4) defines as limiting exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.
16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)(A) requires public meeting notice when more than 25 directly affected landowners would be entitled to receive notice of the application. The rule's purpose is to provide affected landowners a meaningful opportunity to attend a public meeting, review alternatives, provide information, identify community values, and affect route development before route decisions are fixed in an application.

Ill. APPLICABLE PURA AND TAC STANDARDS
PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to determine whether a proposed
transmission project is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or
safety of the public. The statute requires consideration of adequacy of existing service,
need for additional service, effect of granting the certificate on the recipient and any
electric utility serving the proximate area, community values, recreational and park
areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, probable improvement of
service or lowering of cost, and other factors including whether the proposed line will
serve an underserved area.
16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) implements these routing factors and requires consideration
of community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values,
environmental integrity, engineering constraints, costs, and whether the route parallels
existing compatible rights-of-way or property lines. The rule also incorporates prudent
avoidance, which 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(4) defines as limiting exposures to electric and
magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.
16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)(A) requires public meeting notice when more than 25 directly
affected landowners would be entitled to receive notice of the application. The rule's
purpose is to provide affected landowners a meaningful opportunity to attend a public
meeting, review alternatives, provide information, identify community values, and affect
route development before route decisions are fixed in an application.
